oneonone.text:
Growth, postmortem and ingestion proposal check-in

Weekly check-in with Daniela. We talked about my wish to own design work, and agreed on a one-pager for the ingestion redesign by Friday and stronger postmortem contributing factors. Ownership of the ingestion redesign was parked until Daniela checks for overlap with Priya's team.

## Action items

- [ ] Draft a one-pager on the ingestion redesign (problem, a couple of options, rough estimate) and send it to Daniela by Friday; tell her if it slips to Monday (me)
- [ ] Pull the alerting gap out into its own contributing-factors section in the billing postmortem (me)
- [ ] Add the out-of-date rollback runbook to the postmortem as an action item (me)
- [ ] Update the rollback runbook, maybe by end of next week (me)
- [ ] Ask Joaquin for the ingestion cluster throughput metrics; Daniela said he can spare about 20 minutes (me)
- [ ] Look into the blocked ingestion work with Priya's team (Daniela)

## Career growth

- I feel I'm treading water: closing tickets on the same kind of work (integrations, bug fixes, occasional migrations) for about eight months.
  - I want to design systems, not only build what others design.
  - I'd like to own a design doc end to end. I did a small part on the retry logic doc last spring, and Marcus praised it in review.
- Daniela thinks I have the instincts and need more scope.
- I asked how to request this without sounding like I want to skip grunt work. Daniela said the grunt work is part of it and suggested being explicit, for example saying I want to own a specific project by Q3.
- Possible target: the event ingestion redesign, which has been in the backlog.
  - Daniela wants to check for overlap with Priya's team first. Her team is mostly on the downstream consumers.
- Staff track: no promise. It depends on how the ingestion work goes and whether I can show cross-team scope. Leading the proposal would be a strong signal. Daniela framed it as an opportunity, not a test.

## Billing service postmortem

- The billing rollout went out Tuesday, mostly smoothly. A smaller cache issue was caught in staging.
- Daniela likes the root cause section but wants the contributing factors sharper.
  - Decided: the alerting gap gets its own section. It did not fire for about 40 minutes.
  - I was hesitant because it reflects on the on-call setup, which Dev owns. Daniela said the postmortem is about preventing the next incident, not assigning blame.
- Decided: add the out-of-date rollback runbook to the doc as an action item with an owner. I'll take it.

## Ingestion redesign proposal

- Decided: a one-pager by Friday, written for Daniela first. Write it so Marcus could read it cold. Daniela will decide who else sees it.
- I don't have exact current throughput numbers. Daniela said rough numbers are fine if I flag what I don't know.

## Open questions

- Is the ingestion redesign mine to own by Q3? Daniela wants to check for overlap with Priya's team before committing.
- Does the proposal lead to a staff track path? Daniela can't promise it.

hiring.text:
Rahul Venkataraman senior backend debrief

Panel debrief on Rahul Venkataraman's four interview rounds. We agreed to move forward to reference checks, with the attrition comment from the hiring manager chat as the main thing to probe.

## Action items

- [ ] Contact the recruiter today for Rahul's reference list: two former managers and one peer (me)

## System design round

- Strong hire signal (Priya).
  - Asked about write volume first, then drew the event store partitioning without prompting.
  - Explained rebalance handling clearly: backpressure and idempotent consumers.
  - Said he'd check failover semantics before committing to a broker he hadn't run in production. Priya liked that.

## Coding round 1

- Mixed, leaning no hire on coding (Dmitri).
  - Solved the interval merge problem but took a while and went down a wrong path for about ten minutes. He talked through his thinking aloud.
  - Didn't finish the concurrent cache eviction problem. Structure and locking were mostly right, but he ran out of time and got tangled on a race condition walkthrough.

## Coding round 2

- Lean hire (Imani).
  - Finished both problems with clean code and tests, and wrote the tests before being asked.
  - Asked few clarifying questions and started building right away. He handled an edge case Imani had planned to raise, but Imani wasn't sure he would have caught it unprompted.
  - Imani would want to know more about how he scopes work before calling it a strong hire.

## Hiring manager chat

- Positive on culture and motivation (Lena).
  - Wants to leave his current job to build new things. He has done mostly maintenance on a monolith for two years. It's not about money.
  - Disagreed with his last manager on a rewrite and lost. He accepted that but said he would have pushed harder on one part. He was honest about this.
  - Mentioned attrition on his last team and implied he was part of why people left, then moved on quickly. Lena couldn't tell if this was humility or a real issue.
  - Priya didn't cover team dynamics in her round. She said it's worth asking about, though not a dealbreaker.

## Decision and reference checks

- Decided: move forward to reference checks.
  - Focus on the attrition comment, how he worked with the team, and whether people on that team would want to work with him again.
  - Also ask references how he handles being on the losing side of a technical argument.

## Open questions

- Was the attrition comment humility or a real issue? Reference checks should clarify this.
- Does he scope work well enough to be a strong hire? Imani wants more evidence.

sales.text:
Lintly pilot discussion with Harbor Freight Logistics

Harbor Freight's ops lead, Marcus, and their security lead reviewed Lintly's fit and data handling. Harbor Freight wants a six-week pilot with the platform team, but their procurement policy requires SOC 2 Type II, which Lintly won't have until October. The pilot start is tentatively the 7th, pending confirmation.

## Action items

- [ ] Send the SOC 2 Type I report and pen test summary to Marcus today (me)
- [ ] Check with the compliance person about a bridge letter from our auditor, and follow up by Thursday (me)
- [ ] Confirm whether on-prem scoping for Enterprise is worth doing (me)
- [ ] Put a tentative hold on the 7th for pilot kickoff (me)
- [ ] Add the optional pre-commit hook to the pilot setup doc (me)
- [ ] Get approval for a pilot rate and send a quote for 39 Business seats before Thursday (me)
- [ ] Send the follow-up email after the call (me)
- [ ] Confirm the 7th as the start date and the pilot group with the platform lead (Marcus)
- [ ] Ask legal whether the Type II policy is strict and whether a bridge letter is acceptable (Marcus)

## Current review process

- Around 45 engineers across platform, routing and contractors; code review is slow.
- Reviews wait about 3 days for a first review, then another day or two of back-and-forth.
- Senior reviewers spend time on style, naming, unused imports and unhandled errors instead of logic.
- Most CI runs on Jenkins, which often times out. The mobile driver app team uses GitHub Actions. Whether to consolidate is a separate decision.
- Earlier linters were turned off because they produced about 900 warnings on day one.

## Lintly fit

- Lintly only surfaces findings the team has chosen to enforce, ranked by severity.
- Warn-only mode annotates PRs without blocking merges.
- A baseline scan suppresses existing findings, so only new issues in a PR show up. Legacy issues get worked down on the team's schedule.
- Works with both Jenkins and GitHub Actions.

## Pricing

- Per active developer seat per month, billed annually:
  - Team: $22. Core rules, Jenkins and Actions integrations, standard support.
  - Business: $38. Adds custom rule authoring, SSO, and audit logs.
  - Enterprise: custom. Adds on-prem deployment and a dedicated success manager.
- 45 seats on Business is about $1,710 a month, or about $20,400 a year.
- Only developers who opened or commented on a PR in the last 30 days count as active.
  - Six of the 45 are contractors, and two are leaving at month end, so about 39 seats is more realistic.
- Business and up includes SAML and SCIM with Okta, so provisioning is automatic.
- Audit logs are in Business and can be exported to a SIEM.

## Security and data

- Lintly analyzes code in memory and keeps only findings metadata, not source code.
- Customer code is not used for model training, per the terms and DPA.
- Lintly has SOC 2 Type I, obtained in March. The Type II observation window runs through the end of Q3, with the report expected in October.
- Harbor Freight's policy requires Type II for any vendor with source code access, which is a problem. Marcus is unsure whether a current Type I plus a bridge letter would be accepted.
- On-prem is Enterprise only, takes a few weeks to set up, and would keep code inside Harbor Freight's VPC. Marcus said it could be the blocker if legal rejects SaaS-only.
- Secrets detection is part of the security rule pack. It catches common credential patterns and high-entropy strings, and works alongside a vault or GitHub push protection.
  - It can block PR merges. It only blocks local commits with the optional pre-commit hook, which Harbor Freight wants on.

## Pilot plan

- Scope: the platform team only, about 8 to 10 people, for six weeks.
- Success metrics, set up front: review cycle time (the VP's main number), style-related review comments, and end-of-pilot developer sentiment.
  - Baseline from Jenkins and GitHub data in the first week.
- Warn-only for at least the first two weeks, then possibly blocking on security-category findings only.
- Start is tentatively the 7th, because of a release freeze in the first week of the month. The freeze covers prod deploys only.
  - Agreed to treat the first week as setup and leave it out of adoption metrics.

## Open questions

- Will legal accept a current Type I report plus a bridge letter, or does it require Type II?
- If legal rejects SaaS-only, is on-prem worth scoping now?
- Is the 7th confirmed as the start date, and which team members are in the pilot?
- Pilot rate: Harbor Freight wants the first six weeks at half price for a line-item approval. Lintly still needs to approve that rate.

planning.text:
Q1 planning sync: feature scope decisions

We narrowed the Q1 candidates to five and made calls on most of them. Offline sync is the Q1 headline, scoped to last-writer-wins with conflict copies. AI summaries are still open, pending cost numbers.

## Action items

- [ ] Write the Notion and Evernote import deferral, with the nested-tables reason, into the roadmap doc (me)
- [ ] Confirm the offline sync scope (last-writer-wins with conflict copies) with leadership (me)
- [ ] Add the duplicate-notes behavior to the offline sync spec as a release-notes requirement (me)
- [ ] Keep the offline sync spec moving this week so Aiko can scope the conflict copy logic (me)
- [ ] Bring AI summary cost numbers to the next sync (me)
- [ ] Block an hour Thursday afternoon to review the template gallery empty state (me)
- [ ] Show the template gallery empty state by Thursday (Sven)
- [ ] Get lazy-loaded thumbnails done by the 20th, the checkpoint for the end-of-January external beta (Aiko)

## Template gallery

- Backend is merged behind a flag. Ready for internal dogfooding this week.
  - Thumbnail lazy loading is still open, about half a day of work.
  - Sven's mockups reuse the search card component.
- Decided: external beta targets the end of January, with the 20th as the lazy-loading checkpoint.
  - Aiko said end of January is tight but doable if lazy loading is done by the 20th.

## Notion and Evernote import

- Decided: deferred to Q2.
  - The Evernote export format is messy, and the nested tables are the main problem.
  - Aiko didn't want to ship an importer that loses formatting.

## Offline sync

- Reading offline is mostly a reliability issue, since the cache isn't guaranteed. Editing with reconciliation is the real project.
- The main user ask is editing offline and syncing on reconnect. Support tickets point to this.
  - About 40% of last quarter's sync tickets were "I lost my edit" or "my note showed the old version."
- Full CRDT text merging is estimated at 6 to 8 engineer weeks for the core, plus 3 to 4 weeks for mobile clients.
- Decided: Q1 headline is last-writer-wins with a visible conflict copy, about 3 to 4 engineer weeks.
  - Aiko's recommendation is to revisit proper merging in Q2 if the data supports it.
- Known downside: if the title and body are edited in different places on two devices, the copy approach creates two notes. Acceptable for v1 if the release notes say so.
- Design: about 2 weeks for the conflict screen, plus about a week of usability testing.
  - Sven proposed showing both versions side by side so the user can pick or merge, rather than a "conflict detected" modal.
  - Sven sketched three status options: a quiet cloud icon, an offline banner, or a per-note indicator.

## Sharing permissions

- Current model is owner, editor, and viewer. People are confused about editor access through a folder versus direct sharing.
- Decided: minimal version only. One effective-permission display, about 2 weeks of engineering and about 1 week of design.
  - Example: "Jordan can edit because they're in the Team Notes folder."
- Decided: enterprise SSO group mapping and audit logs are deferred, with no date committed for Q2.
  - Aiko said those are a separate project.
  - Sales will likely push back, so we'll say we'll scope it in Q2 before promising a date.

## PDF export

- Decided: in for Q1.
  - The HTML styling engine already exists, so this is mostly wiring it to a renderer. About a week, possibly more if fonts are a problem.

## iOS quick-capture widget

- Decided: in for Q1, iOS only, about 2 weeks.
  - Android widgets are fragile right now, so Aiko would rather not do both at once.
  - Sven said iOS-first is fine as long as we don't hide that Android is coming. Many of the target users are on iOS.

## AI summaries

- Concern: per-user inference cost could be significant, the margin is unknown, and summaries of messy notes may be poor quality.
  - I think a pilot is worth doing. Aiko thinks it should not be in Q1 at all.
  - Aiko wants at least a month of cost modeling and a small user test first.
- Sven doesn't want to design a summary card before there's evidence. Sven suggested a fake summary button that leads to a waitlist to measure interest.
  - The waitlist test is agreed as a test, not a committed Q1 feature.
- Not resolved whether AI pilot engineering gets Q1 time. Revisit at the next sync with cost numbers.

## Open questions

- Should the AI summary pilot get any Q1 engineering time?
- Will leadership accept offline sync as last-writer-wins rather than full merging?
- When do we revisit proper merging for offline sync in Q2?

brainstorm.text:
Booking app name and positioning brainstorm

We brainstormed product names and taglines for the booking app and did not decide anything. Topout, Slab and Rackly are the main candidates, and we will revisit on Thursday once the trademark results are in.

## Action items

- [ ] Pull trademark searches for Topout and Slab and send them round tonight (me)
- [ ] Try taglines that don't lead with failure, avoiding lines like "never get turned away" (Dani)
- [ ] Ask my mom about Beta again (Dani)

## Name candidates

- Topout is the leading option: it's the word for finishing a climb and implies getting to the top.
  - Someone thinks a gym management company may already use it, and it may sound like a sports drink. Needs a trademark check.
- Slab is short and a climbing term for a steep flat wall, but it may sound like a flooring company or a bakery.
- Rackly has a fan (Tomás), though it may sound like a boat rental.
- Beta is parked: it's climbing jargon but also means a test version, which may confuse people outside climbing.
- Cragline is parked: it sounds like an airline. We agreed to avoid transport-sounding words.
- Dropped: Crux, Send and Clip (taken), Access (too generic), Kit and Gear (too vague or generic), Basecamp (project management software).
- Belay leans toward feature names, not the product name, because outsiders may not know how to pronounce it. Feature ideas: "Belay alerts" for notifications, "belay queue" for the waitlist.

## Positioning

- The main problem is that gyms have route-setting schedules and walls that open, and people don't know when a spot is free, so they show up and get turned away.
- The name should lean toward booking and access, and the tagline can do the climbing work.
- There are two audiences: gym owners, who pay and sign the contract, and climbers, who use the app and spread it. The name has to work for both.
- The promise may be "you'll actually get on the wall," which is more specific than "book," since booking is the mechanism. Someone suggested the name could be a verb for getting on the wall.

## Taglines

- "Never get turned away at the door" is a strong line but leads with the failure state.
- "Book your wall" sounds like a hotel chain ad to some of us.
- Taglines are parked until we settle on a name.

## Open questions

- Is Topout already trademarked in a related field?
- Is Slab too close to a flooring or bakery name?
- How do people say Belay (bee-lay or buh-lay)?
- Should Beta be kept? Dani's mom is the test case.

customer_support.text:
Offline sync failure escalation and workaround

The call covered field jobs that fail to sync after going offline on app 4.11.3. A repro was confirmed. I'm escalating it to the sync team and sending billing the re-dispatch request, but no fix date or credit was committed.

## Action items

- [ ] Escalate the sync failure to the sync team today with the repro steps, flagged as affecting the northeast region and the 4.11.3 rollout (me)
- [ ] Send the billing escalation today with Marcus's re-dispatch figures and the 41 of 163 report, copying Marcus (me)
- [ ] Include the repro steps and version numbers in the billing email (me)
- [ ] Send Marcus's team a short written version of the workaround (me)
- [ ] Try the workaround on more test jobs over the next day before relying on it (Dev Patel)

## Problem

- Field jobs that go offline show as complete on the phone, but on the web dashboard they are missing, partly there (checklist without photos), or stuck at pending sync.
- Marcus estimated about one in four offline jobs is affected. A report from Thursday showed 41 of 163 jobs for that week incomplete on the server.
- Marcus's first complaints came around the 10th, two days after the update went out on the 8th.
- Two reinstalls and a full wipe of one phone have not helped.
- Marcus says technicians can't close out jobs and are being asked to babysit their phones.

## Repro

- Dev reproduced it with airplane mode on: created a job, filled the checklist, took two photos, got a signature, then turned airplane mode off.
- The device showed it as synced. On the web dashboard the job was there but had no photos.
- Photos were confirmed on the device, so the device side appears to record correctly and the server side is not receiving or is dropping attachments.
- I said I don't want to claim a root cause yet.

## Workaround

- Keep the app in the foreground for about 30 seconds after reconnecting, then force a manual sync from the job menu.
- This worked on the one test job Dev tried (test two).
- Decided: Use this workaround for now. I said one success isn't proof.
- Marcus called it a band-aid, not a fix.

## Credit and billing

- Marcus estimates $9,000 to $11,000 in labor lost to re-dispatches over the past two weeks. He wants a credit on this invoice, not a discount on next year's price.
- I can't approve a credit or refund. That decision belongs to billing, so I can't commit to an amount or outcome on this call.
- Marcus has a contract renewal in three weeks and is considering whether to keep paying full price.

## Open questions

- Whether billing will approve a credit, and how much.
- Root cause of the server-side attachment loss, and when a fix will ship.

design_review.text:
Payouts job queue move from Redis to Postgres

The design review covered moving settlement retries off Redis and onto Postgres with SKIP LOCKED. The group agreed on settlement moving to Postgres, with fanout staying on Redis for now, and a prototype is gated on answers to two open questions and on load test numbers.

## Action items

- [ ] Pull the client error logs for both Redis eviction incident windows and post them in the doc by Thursday the 23rd (me)
- [ ] Run a load test on the local idempotency table by March 28 (me)
- [ ] Write up the review in the doc and tag owners (me)
- [ ] Check whether the Go driver uses prepared statements under pgbouncer transaction pooling, by the 18th (Ola)
- [ ] Review the pgbouncer pool config for long-running holds and session-level state (owner unclear)
- [ ] Ping the processor account team about the real idempotency window (owner unclear)
- [ ] Own the decision doc on moving fanout off Redis by the end of next sprint, March 14 (Greg)

## Settlement move to Postgres

Decided: Settlement retries move to Postgres with SKIP LOCKED, using polling with backoff from 50 ms up to 500 ms when the queue is empty.
- Card processor retries are about 90% of volume. Internal fanout is small but latency sensitive.
- Motivation: two Redis incidents last quarter where evicted keys silently dropped jobs; no transactional enqueue, so a crash between the Postgres commit and the Redis write can leave ghost payout state; Postgres with pgbouncer already runs in production, so no new stateful system.
- Current p99 end to end is about 40 ms. Expected p99 on Postgres is about 120 ms, which is not confirmed.

## Idempotency

Decided: Use a local idempotency table keyed on job ID, storing the processor response, rather than relying on the processor's dedupe window.
- The processor call happens outside the transaction: lock, mark in_progress, commit, call the processor with the job ID, then mark complete in a second transaction.
- The sales deck says the processor window is 24 hours, but retries can go out to about three days. A retry after the window could double charge, which is a money issue.
- Storing the response also allows replaying the outcome without calling the processor again.

## Throughput and load

- Peak is about 340 payouts per second over the last month.
- The local table adds one insert and one update per job, about 700 extra writes per second at peak, on top of queue traffic.
- Not load tested yet. Decided: no production greenlight until load test numbers are in.

## Fanout

- Decided: Webhook fanout stays on Redis for now.
- Two systems is worse operationally, so fanout should be revisited after the Kafka consumer group work settles.
- Concern about adding Kafka topics now, since consumer lag alerts have been noisy.

## Rollback and reconciliation

- Plan is dual-write for one week, enqueuing to both systems but consuming from one. Rollback means flipping the consumer.
- Dual-write doubles enqueue cost, which is considered cheap, but divergence could cause jobs to run twice or never run.
- The nightly reconciliation job compares both sides by job ID. Priya's team owns it, but it is built for the ledger, not the queue, which is a gap.

## Driver and pgbouncer

- Transaction pooling breaks session-level state such as advisory locks and prepared statements.
- Unclear whether the Go driver uses prepared statements by default. The simple protocol may be set, but this is not in the doc.
- If the driver caches prepared statements under transaction pooling, errors can look random.

## Open questions

- Is the real processor idempotency window 24 hours? Not confirmed by their account team.
- Does the Go driver use prepared statements under our pool config?
- Was the Redis eviction root cause real eviction, or a client swallowing noeviction OOM errors?
- Is the p99 of about 120 ms acceptable for the path that remains on Postgres?

numbers.text:
Q3 operating review and vendor renewals

The meeting covered Q3 spend, revenue, cash, headcount, payroll and vendor renewals ahead of the board pack. We decided to keep three open backfills and close two, to call the storage overage "under review" without a number, and to footnote the payables push. The analytics platform renewal decision is still open, with a deadline of October 15.

## Action items

- [ ] Check in the HR system that the approved headcount plan is 228, not 230, and send Hannah a correction today if needed (me)
- [ ] Raise right-sizing the expense management tool seats at the January review (me)
- [ ] Send the list of orphaned storage snapshots before the variance memo is finalized (Priya)
- [ ] Pull the billing schedule to size the revenue pull-forward by Thursday (Dan)
- [ ] Check the 2.97M payroll planning figure against the final Q4 hire dates (Dan)

## Q3 actuals

- Operating spend was 4.87M against a 4.61M budget, about 260K (5.6%) over.
  - Cloud is about 140K over, mostly a storage tier still running after the migration.
  - Contractors are about 95K over because two data engineers were extended through September.
- Storage overage is still unconfirmed as orphaned or in use.
  - Decided: call it "under review" in the memo and don't commit to a number until Priya's list is in.
- Recognized revenue was 11.2M against a 10.9M forecast, up about 2.8%.
  - Mostly from the Halverson and Brightline enterprise renewals, which closed early in August.
  - Hannah guessed about a third of the pull-forward is timing, but it shouldn't go to the board until checked against the billing schedule.
- Cash ended at 6.3M, up from 5.1M at the end of Q2.
  - About 380K of the increase is payables pushed past quarter end, mostly to two vendors moved from net-45 to net-60 by written agreement.
  - Decided: footnote the payables push in the deck, since it flatters the cash number.

## Headcount

- 212 filled roles against an approved plan of 228, so 16 open. Eleven are in active interview loops.
- Five are backfills, and the recruiter needs a decision on keeping their posts live through November.
  - The search firm retainer is about 18K a month across all of them.
  - Decided: keep three backfills open and close two, the finance analyst and the second support lead.
  - The support lead gap can be covered by the current team through the holidays.

## Payroll run rate

- Current fully loaded payroll is 2.7M a month. The 2.4M figure was last quarter's, before the Q2 hires.
- Adding the 16 open roles at average loaded cost brings full plan to roughly 2.95 to 3.0M a month.
  - Planning figure is 2.97M, shown as 3.0M in the deck.

## Vendor renewals

- Analytics platform renews November 14 at 430K a year. Non-renewal notice is 30 days, so the decision is due by October 15.
  - Three-year term: 3% discount, about 417K a year.
  - One-year term: 7% uplift, 460K.
  - The gap is about 43K a year. The three-year term is risky while the reporting stack is still changing and we might switch tools in year two.
- Expense management tool renews December 1 at 88K a year. The 60-day notice window has passed, so it auto-renews.
  - About 150 seats are licensed, but only about 60 are active monthly (roughly 40% adoption).
  - Seats can only be right-sized at the next renewal.
- Insurance renewal is in March and not urgent.
- Hosting provider SLA dispute: about 22K in credits owed for the August outage.
  - The outage lasted 94 minutes against a 60-minute SLA. They say it was within their tolerance window.
  - Dan is handling it. Escalate to their account manager if there's no movement by month end.

## Open questions

- Should the analytics platform go on a one-year or three-year term?
- How much of the revenue pull-forward reverses in Q4?
- What is the actual storage cost: orphaned snapshots or in use?
